response.query: How should ecological thresholds (B/Bmsy, F/Fmsy) and climate variability be formalized as policy triggers within a coupled bioeconomic–econometric model?
response.answer: Ecological thresholds (B/Bmsy, F/Fmsy) and climate variability should be formalized as policy triggers in a coupled bioeconomic–econometric model by setting specific limits and using climate projections to adjust management strategies.

results.title: Overfished, overfishing, and rebuilding stocks - Sustainable Fisheries UW
results.content: A conservative estimate says at least 82% of wild-caught fish come from fisheries with healthy populations. We all want to eat fish from MSY-maintained populations, but can fish from a depleted, or overfished, population ever be sustainable? If the proportion of fish caught (F) is greater than FMSY, overfishing is happening. Fishing mortality is usually given as a ratio of **F/FMSY**; a ratio over 1 means overfishing. Overfished refers to the **biomass (B)** of a population, or stock, of fish. If the biomass of fish in the water is well below BMSY, the stock is overfished, or depleted. According to the UN FAO, a ratio under 0.8 signifies an overfished fishery; however the USA typically defines an overfished fishery as any with B/BMSY below 0.5. If the government is legally mandated to assist overfished fisheries (as the USA is), it makes sense to help fisheries that are significantly depleted instead of those that may be on the downswing of a natural cycle. We typically refer to overfished as anything with a B/Bmsy below 0.8, but you should know that not all of these fisheries are in dire shape. We can plot the F/Fmsy ratio against the B/Bmsy ratio to get a sense of the sustainability of a fishery. Fisheries with B/Bmsy below 1 (overfished), but with F/Fmsy also below 1 (underfishing), are **rebuilding**. The fishery is not at the right population level, but fishing pressure is low enough that B will continue to increase. If a fishery is overfished, shouldn’t we stop fishing (F/Fmsy =0) it to let the population recover? In some cases of significant depletion, fishery managers have closed a fishery to rebuild, but remember—fishery management has multiple goals, one of which is to ensure well-being for people who depend on a fishery being open, e.g. fishermen and women can’t simply not work for a year. Fortunately, fish stocks can rebuild quickly even without closing fisheries because they evolved to reproduce quickly. With the right management, fisheries around the world can rebuild in just a short amount of time—we are already seeing it with so many stocks rebuilt from the depleted years of the 1980s & 1990s. Of the world’s fisheries, 69% are sustainably managed.
